findings.claim: All electrical installation work in the UK must comply with BS 7671 (the IET Wiring Regulations), and qualified electricians are responsible for testing and certifying that the work is safe before a building is occupied.
findings.truth: BS 7671 is a widely used non-statutory standard. Electrical work must be done by competent people; compliance with BS 7671 is likely to meet relevant electricity-at-work requirements, but it is not a universal legal requirement.
findings.evidence: HSE, Electrical safety FAQ; HSE, Electricity at Work Regulations guidance

findings.claim: must comply with BS 7671 (the IET Wiring Regulations) and certify that completed work is safe before the building is occupied
findings.truth: The answer should describe competence and relevant safety requirements. BS 7671 is a widely used standard, not a universal statutory requirement.
findings.evidence: HSE, Electrical safety FAQ; HSE, Electricity at Work Regulations guidance

findings.claim: What must an electrician comply with when installing electrical services in a new building?
findings.truth: BS 7671 is a widely used standard for electrical installations, rather than an unconditional requirement for every electrical installation.

findings.claim: Sites must be securely fenced and clearly signed to prevent unauthorised access by members of the public, including children.
findings.truth: The principal contractor must take steps to prevent unauthorised access. Secure fencing and clear signs are examples, but are not prescribed for every site.
findings.evidence: HSE, Principal contractors: roles and responsibilities

findings.claim: The Health and Safety at Work Act (1974) is the cornerstone of workplace safety law in the UK.
findings.truth: The 1974 Act is the main workplace safety law in Great Britain. It does not extend to Northern Ireland, where the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978 is the primary legislation.
findings.evidence: spec 1.8.3 footnote 4; legislation.gov.uk, Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 s84; nidirect, Employers’ health and safety responsibilities

findings.claim: Under this Act, employers in construction are legally required to prepare risk assessments
findings.truth: The 1974 Act sets general duties. The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 make the risk-assessment requirement explicit; the specification describes the listed duties as requirements of health and safety regulations.
findings.evidence: spec 1.8.3; HSE, Managing risks and risk assessment at work

findings.claim: it is illegal for an unregistered person to carry out any work on gas appliances or pipework
findings.truth: A person carrying out gas work as part of a business must be competent and Gas Safe registered. The law allows consumers to carry out limited user tasks that do not disturb gas-carrying components or combustion.
findings.evidence: Gas Safe Register, Who can legally work on a gas appliance?

findings.claim: For electrical installation, inspection and testing, the relevant accreditation scheme is NICEIC
findings.truth: Electrical work must be carried out by competent people. NICEIC is one certification scheme that assesses electrical businesses; it is not an accreditation every electrician must hold.
findings.evidence: spec 1.8.5; HSE, Electricity – Systems in buildings; NICEIC, Approved Contractor scheme; NICEIC Help Hub

findings.claim: All services must be isolated before work begins
findings.truth: Services should normally be isolated before work. Live electrical work is permitted only in limited circumstances after it is shown unreasonable for the work to be done dead and suitable precautions are taken.
findings.evidence: spec 1.8.5; HSE, Electrical safety FAQ; HSE, Electricity at Work Regulations guidance

findings.claim: An enclosed space is any area that is fully or partially enclosed, not designed for people to work in on a regular basis
findings.truth: A confined or enclosed space is a fully or partly enclosed place where there is a foreseeable risk of serious injury from hazardous substances or dangerous conditions. Being designed for continuous occupancy is not part of the legal definition.
findings.evidence: HSE, Safe work in confined spaces; spec 1.8.6

findings.claim: On construction sites, enclosed spaces include manholes, culverts, storage tanks, sewers, ductwork and deep excavations.
findings.truth: Those places can be enclosed spaces only where their enclosed nature creates a foreseeable specified risk. A deep excavation is not automatically an enclosed space.
findings.evidence: HSE, Safe work in confined spaces; spec 1.8.6

findings.claim: Workers must use atmospheric monitoring equipment to test air quality before entering and while working
findings.truth: Testing and monitoring are required where the risk assessment identifies an unsafe or potentially changing atmosphere. The competent person defines the testing and monitoring needed in the safe system of work.
findings.evidence: HSE, Safe work in confined spaces, paras 89–92

findings.claim: a trained attendant must remain outside the space at all times
findings.truth: Suitable rescue arrangements must be in place before entry. They depend on the risk assessment; guidance says someone should normally attend outside to communicate, raise the alarm and take charge of rescue, rather than imposing that exact arrangement in every case.
findings.evidence: spec 1.8.6; HSE, Safe work in confined spaces; HSE, Health and safety in construction HSG150

findings.claim: writing "a qualified person" alone is not specific enough to earn the mark
findings.truth: The specification names Gas Safe as an example of an accreditation but does not prescribe mark-credit rules for this wording. Either retain this as house guidance without a mark claim, or support it with the relevant published mark scheme.

findings.claim: do not write "health and safety law" alone, as this is too vague to earn the mark
findings.truth: The specification gives the assessment format and subject content but no mark-credit rule for this wording. Either recast the advice as a study recommendation or support it with the relevant published mark scheme.

findings.claim: examiners frequently award marks for naming the specific access methods
findings.truth: The specification requires learners to understand appropriate methods of access but does not state a frequency or mark award for naming them. Either recast this as study advice or support it with the relevant published mark scheme.

findings.claim: An untrained bystander ... will almost certainly be overcome themselves ... the majority of the victims were would-be rescuers.
findings.truth: HSE guidance supports the risk of a second casualty and says the second person is often a would-be rescuer, but the fetched sources do not support the probability claims. Either qualify them to ‘may’ and ‘often’, or provide a source for the statistics.
findings.evidence: HSE, Managing confined spaces on farms; HSE, Health and safety in construction HSG150

summary: Verified corrections address legal scope, statutory duties, accreditation, isolation and confined-space safety. Four exam or probability claims need an editorial decision because the accessible specification and sources do not support their absolute wording.
